name: Vasa Museum
label: Vasa Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Galärparken' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Galärparken' (way/236128556): middle (312 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/27288534: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Vasa Museum' (198 m across).

text.description:
The Vasa Museum (Vasamuseet) sits on the island of Djurgården and houses the 64-gun warship Vasa, which sank on her maiden voyage in 1628. It is the only almost fully intact 17th-century ship ever salvaged. The museum opened on 15 June 1990, and from outside it is easy to pick out. A large copper roof carries stylised masts that show how tall Vasa stood when fully rigged. Some of the walls are clad in wooden panels painted dark red, blue, tar black, ochre yellow and dark green, which gives you colour and texture to work with.

The best outdoor photo is from the waterfront edge of Galärparken, a free, leafy park right beside the museum. From there you see the roofline and masts with boats moored in the harbour in front. Four other museum ships lie in that harbour: the ice breaker Sankt Erik, the lightvessel Finngrundet, the torpedo boat Spica and the rescue boat Bernhard Ingelsson. They make good foreground interest. Leave a little space around the roof and masts so the shape reads clearly. Photographing the ship itself means going inside, where it can be seen from six levels. Check the official site for photo rules and ticket details before you go.
text.geographic_location: On the island of Djurgården in Stockholm, on the harbour waterfront.
text.directions_text: Head for the island of Djurgården in Stockholm and look for the Vasa Museum. From there the museum's middle is to the north-west, about 2 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole roofline with the boats in front. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and the roof and masts will not fit. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the masts and roof detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Galärparken (waterfront edge of the park, facing the museum). The museum's striking copper roof and the boats moored in the harbour in front of it. The museum lies to the north-west. From here the photo shows the museum's copper roof and the boats moored in the harbour in front of it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the roofline along the upper third, with the moored boats along the bottom. Keep the phone level so the masts stand upright. If you want an alternative, the museum's front exterior shows the copper bowsprit above the roof, with the harbour and vintage ships behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the roof to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out the copper. Take a few shots at different zoom levels, because telephoto and the default lens (1x) give quite different results here.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Softer morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the roof and the water. Midday sun can cause glare off the harbour.

text.access_note: Galärparken is a free public park, but entry to the museum itself is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning or late-afternoon light is generally softer and gives less glare off the water than midday sun.
Lowering the exposure slider helps stop a bright sky washing out the roof.

name: Gamla Stan and Stortorget
label: Stortorget
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/332635708: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Stortorget' (76 m across).
notes: The coloured houses on the square.

text.description: Stortorget, the "Grand Square", is the oldest square in Stockholm and the historic heart of Gamla Stan, the old town. It never was a grand showpiece. The buildings around it were added gradually and a little haphazardly, which gives the square an uneven, lived-in look that suits photos well. The northern side is taken up by the Stock Exchange Building (Börshuset), designed by Erik Palmstedt and built between 1773 and 1776. Its rounded corner and lantern-style cupola are easy to spot. Today it houses the Swedish Academy and the Nobel Museum. In the square itself there is an old well, also by Palmstedt. Around the edges you will find tall, colourful town houses. One of them, number 3 (Grillska huset), has cloverleaf-shaped gables added in 1718 and a blue façade. The square is known for its Christmas market, when it is busy and full of colour. For a good photo, include a little of the cobbled ground in the foreground so the viewer feels the size of the space. Then let the façades fill the rest. Keep the phone level so the vertical lines of the buildings stay straight. If you want a close-up, look for the gables and the rounded corner of the Stock Exchange Building. Right next to it: Stockholm Cathedral (Storkyrkan). Right next to it: German Church.
text.geographic_location: Stortorget is in the middle of Gamla Stan, the old town in central Stockholm, on the plateau of the island of Stadsholmen. The Stock Exchange Building stands on its northern side.
text.directions_text: Head for Gamla Stan, the old town in central Stockholm, and continue on foot. The square lies in the middle of the island. The phone icon on the map is about 10 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the width of the square and the façades in one frame. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the gables and the cupola.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 10 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the edges of the buildings with the vertical lines to keep them straight. Keep a strip of cobbles at the bottom of the frame for depth. Then take a second shot with the telephoto, focused on the Stock Exchange Building or a single gabled house.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest façade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky and the colours do not wash out. In the evening or at the Christmas market, try night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning usually means fewer people in the frame. In the evening, with the lights on, the square looks warmer, and night mode works well then.

text.access_note: Stortorget is a public square; the Nobel Museum and other buildings around it may have their own opening rules, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning is usually quieter on the square than later in the day.
In the evening the lighting around the square makes a warm look, and night mode works well then.
Level, straight-on framing helps keep the vertical lines of the buildings straight.

text.description:
ABBA The Museum is an interactive exhibition about the Swedish pop band, on the island of Djurgården in Stockholm. It opened in May 2013 and sits in a building near the Gröna Lund theme park. It is the permanent home of the ABBAWORLD exhibition, which toured Europe and Australia in 2009–2011, and it holds stage costumes donated by the band members. Inside you will find a recreation of the Polar Studio, a section styled on Brighton at the 1974 Eurovision Song Contest, and Benny's self-playing piano, which is linked to the one in his home.

For a phone photographer, the outside of the building is the easy, reliable shot. It is a big, simple subject that sits well in a wide frame, and Djurgården gives it a relaxed, leisurely setting. Find a spot outside with a clear view of the facade and photograph the building as a record of your visit, perhaps with a friend in the foreground. Step back a few paces to fit more of it in, and switch on gridlines so the walls stay straight.

Inside, photography rules can differ from room to room, so look out for signs and check the official site before you go. If photos are allowed, the costumes and studio recreations make good close-up details.
text.geographic_location: On the island of Djurgården in central Stockholm, in a building near the Gröna Lund theme park.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check a local journey planner for the best way to reach Djurgården. Once there, head for Gröna Lund and look for the museum in a building near it. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the building as a whole. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and cannot step back far enough. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for signs and details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Find a spot outside the building with a clear view of the facade, and take a few steps back to fit more in.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the edges of the building with them so the walls look straight. Keep your phone level, as tilting it makes the building lean. If the area is busy, wait a moment for a gap in the crowd, or include a few people for a sense of scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly if the sky is bright, so the walls do not turn washed out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime in even light is easiest. Earlier in the day it is likely to be quieter. If you come in the evening, try night mode and hold the phone steady against something solid.

text.access_note: The museum is a ticketed attraction, so check the official site before you go for entry details and photography rules inside.

name: Djurgården and the Blue Gate
label: Djurgården
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/5695419: large area 'Djurgården' (4826 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description: Djurgården is an island in central Stockholm that mixes forest, meadow, waterfront promenades and old wooden buildings, all within a short distance of the city. This spot covers the island as a whole, with the Blue Gate (Blå Porten), the café at the Liljevalchs art gallery, as one of its landmarks. The island photographs well because the scenes change so quickly. You can have water and boats in one frame, then tall trees, historic buildings or open grass in the next. The island was once a royal game park. Its name comes from King John III's plan of 1579 to keep deer, reindeer and elk there. Later it became a popular place for recreation, and Gröna Lund opened in 1883 and Skansen in 1891. Many buildings in the western part date from the Stockholm World's Fair of 1897. The island is part of the National City Park, founded in 1995. For your pictures, look for a clear foreground such as a path, railing or tree branch, and let the water or the buildings fill the background. Walk a little along the waterfront rather than shooting everything from one place, because the island is large and every stretch looks different. Keep your phone lens clean, as spray and fingerprints soften the picture. If you want the Blue Gate itself, look for the café by the Liljevalchs gallery and take a straight-on shot of its entrance.
text.geographic_location: Djurgården is an island in central Stockholm, with parks, museums and the Gröna Lund amusement park. The Blue Gate (Blå Porten) is the café at the Liljevalchs art gallery on the island.
text.directions_text: Follow the map to Djurgården and use the compass direction south-east. The phone icon on the map is about 1.4 km north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the overall scene. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for close waterfront or park views. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out buildings or boats in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 1.4 km north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on a top or bottom line so the water, trees or sky get the space they deserve. At this distance, try 2x or 3x to pull the island's shoreline and buildings closer, and keep a bit of foreground in the shot for depth. Once you are on the island itself, go back to the default lens (1x) or ultra-wide (0.5x) for paths, gates and shopfronts.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or water to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Hold the phone still with both hands, and try a Live Photo on the water so you can pick the sharpest frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. In midday sun, look for shade under the trees.

text.access_note: Djurgården is an open island with public parks and paths, but individual museums, attractions and the Blue Gate café have their own rules, so check the official sites before you go.

name: Skansen
label: Skansen
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/377977591: large area 'Skansen' (903 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description:
Skansen is Sweden's oldest open-air museum, with a zoo alongside it, on the hill of Djurgården close to the centre of Stockholm. Artur Hazelius opened it on 11 October 1891 to show how people lived in different parts of Sweden before industry changed the country. He bought around 150 houses from across the land and had them rebuilt here, so a single walk takes you from farmhouses of the 16th century to the Skogaholm Manor house of 1680. Staff in traditional dress work in a replica 19th-century town, and the site also has Scandinavian animals such as brown bears, moose and lynx.

For a phone, the appeal is variety. There are old timber buildings, village lanes, hillside paths, farm animals and, in early December, the Christmas market on Bollnäs square, which has run since 1903. Most scenes work well as simple, tidy compositions: a house with a path leading to it, a craftsperson at work, or a wide view of a square. The site covers about 75 acres, so do not try to photograph everything. Pick two or three areas and give each a few minutes. Since the buildings and animals are part of a working museum, stay on the paths and keep out of other visitors' way while you line up a shot.
text.geographic_location: Skansen sits on the hill of Djurgården, the island park-district close to central Stockholm. The site is large, and the subject sits inside it.
text.directions_text: From central Stockholm, head to the island of Djurgården, then go up to the Skansen hill. Skansen is also served by tram line 7 and by the Skansens Bergbana funicular on the northwest side of the hill. The phone icon on the map is about 110 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for buildings and village scenes. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) in tight lanes or open squares, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for animals and craft details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 110 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put a path or fence line on one of the lower lines, so it leads the eye to a building. Include a doorway, a roofline or a person in period dress to give a sense of scale. For animals, zoom in and wait for them to turn their heads.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the main subject to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if bright sky is washing out the sky above the roofs. Try portrait mode for close shots of craftspeople, and Live Photos for moving scenes such as folk dancing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early or late in the day usually gives softer light on the timber buildings and fewer people in your shots. In early December the Christmas market is busy, so keep your phone ready for evening lights.

text.access_note: Skansen is a museum and zoo that is likely to be ticketed with set opening times, so check the official site before you go.

Turn on the gridlines to keep the building upright, and tap on the facade to set focus and exposure before you shoot. Do it quickly, as boats and people move through the frame.

label: City Hall

pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/29368: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Stockholm City Hall' (169 m across).

text.description: Stockholm City Hall (Stadshuset) is the seat of Stockholm Municipality, and it is also where the Nobel Prize banquet is held. It stands on the eastern tip of Kungsholmen, right on the shore of Riddarfjärden, facing Riddarholmen and Södermalm. It photographs well because of the contrast between dark red brick and open water. The site, overlooking Riddarfjärden, inspired a central motif of city architecture set against water. The building went up between 1911 and 1923 and used nearly eight million bricks. Look for the details that soften all that brick: turrets with golden starlets, decorated balconies, wooden masts and statues. The tower is 106 metres high and is topped with the Three Crowns, the Swedish national symbol. It sits at the south-east corner beside the water. The small park between the building and the shore has sculptures by Carl Eldh. These make good foreground subjects, and so does the pillar with the statue of Engelbrekt Engelbrektsson, which faces Riddarholmen. Take a few frames of the brickwork, a balcony and the tower top, then move along the water's edge if you want more of the building in one shot.
text.geographic_location: On the eastern tip of Kungsholmen island, on the northern shore of Riddarfjärden, facing Riddarholmen and Södermalm.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the eastern tip of Kungsholmen. Look for the tall brick tower topped with the Three Crowns beside the water. The phone icon on the map is about 25 m north-east of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for close-up, looking-up shots of the brick walls and tower. Use the default lens (1x) for balanced views. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out turrets, golden starlets, balconies and statues.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 25 m north-east of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. Face south-west and shoot the walls, turrets and details.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and keep the vertical lines of the walls and tower straight, which is easier if you stand square to the wall. Let a sculpture or the water's edge sit in the lower part of the frame for depth. For the whole building with the tower, step back along the waterside and use 0.5x or 1x.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brickwork to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the red brick keeps its colour. Try a Live Photo if boats or people are moving on the water in the background.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is usually kinder to red brick than harsh midday sun. Dusk can also work well, when you can switch to night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or railing.

text.access_note: The building and tower are part of a major tourist attraction and may have access restrictions or ticketed entry, so check the official site before you go.

text.description: Fotografiska is a photography museum housed in a former customs house at Stadsgården, built in 1906 in the Art Nouveau style. It was designed by Ferdinand Boberg and is listed as a building of cultural interest. The museum opened here in 2010 and, as of 2020, drew more than 500,000 visitors a year, so it is a well-known Stockholm address. The building is what makes it worth a photo stop. It is a solid old structure with a strong, characterful outline, and it looks quite different from the modern glass boxes found elsewhere in the city. The phone icon on the map is about 25 m south-west of the subject. From there the building sits to the north-east. Start with a wide view that shows the whole façade and a little of the surroundings, then move in for details such as windows, rooflines and signage. Fotografiska is a working museum with a café, bar and shop, so people will often be passing in front of the entrance. Wait a moment for a clear gap, or include a few figures to give a sense of scale. If you want to go inside, check the official site for entry details before you go.
text.geographic_location: Fotografiska is at Stadsgården in Stockholm, in the former customs house.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Stadsgården area of Stockholm. Fotografiska is the large former customs house there. The phone icon on the map is about 25 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the building. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot fit the whole façade in. Use 2x or the telephoto lens for details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 25 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. Face that way and keep the whole building in view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the building's vertical edges parallel to the vertical lines, so it does not lean. Hold the phone level and at chest height. Take one wide shot of the whole building, then a closer one of a window or entrance detail.

pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/34394: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Royal Palace' (324 m across).

text.description:
Stockholm's Royal Palace is the official residence of the Swedish monarch and is used by the King for representative purposes as head of state. It stands on Stadsholmen in Gamla stan, beside the water of Norrström. The austere Baroque design is by Nicodemus Tessin the Younger. It replaced the medieval Tre Kronor castle, which burned down on 7 May 1697. Building was halted in 1709 because of the Great Northern War and picked up again in 1727. The palace was ready to live in by 1754. Inside are 1,430 rooms, though you'll only be photographing the outside.

It photographs well because the façades are long, regular and symmetrical, so even a quick shot looks tidy and balanced. The pale walls also stand out well against the sky. Include some foreground, such as the open ground in front of you or passing people, to give a sense of scale. Keep your phone level so the long horizontal lines stay straight. For a closer shot, zoom in on the rows of windows and stonework, which repeat in a satisfying pattern. The palace has been undergoing a long façade renovation since 2011, so you may see some scaffolding or covered sections.
text.geographic_location: In the northern part of Gamla stan (the Old Town), on the island of Stadsholmen beside Norrström, next to the Riksdag building.
text.directions_text: Head for Gamla stan, where the palace stands, by taxi or hired scooter, and aim for the north-eastern side of the palace. From there the palace is about 3 minutes on foot to the south-west. The phone icon on the map is about 60 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x). Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the building is too big to fit, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 60 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the roof edge up with a horizontal grid line. Keep some foreground in the shot for scale. For a second shot, zoom to 2x or more and fill the frame with the window rows and carved stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the palace to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the pale walls keep their detail. Panorama mode works if you want the full length of the building, but move slowly and hold the phone upright.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and gentler shadows on the stonework than the middle of the day.

text.access_note: You can photograph the palace's exterior from the surrounding public areas. Check the official palace website for interior and museum visiting information.

text.description: Kungsträdgården, known to locals as Kungsan, is a long, tree-lined park in the middle of Stockholm. In late April its cherry trees turn the paths into a pink tunnel, which makes it one of the city's best-loved spring photo spots. The blossom avenue is the classic frame. Stand underneath and point your phone up into the canopy so the pink flowers sit against the sky. It can get very busy at peak bloom, so go early if you can. For a more layered shot, try oversized wooden chess pieces in the foreground with blossom branches above. Another option is swans on the water with the city buildings behind and a couple on the shore. The park has a long history. It was first recorded in 1430 as the king's cabbage garden and later became a royal pleasure garden. The tree-lined avenues arrived in the 1860s. Molin's Fountain and the statues of Charles XII and Charles XIII are good subjects outside blossom season. In 2004, 285 new linden trees were planted. In winter there is an ice rink, which gives you a different kind of photo. The blossom depends on the spring weather, so timing varies from year to year.
text.geographic_location: Kungsträdgården is in central Stockholm, a short walk from the Royal Palace and the Old Town. Strömgatan quay runs along its southern edge, and Hamngatan with the NK department store lies to the north.
text.directions_text: No stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Old Town and Royal Palace, or from NK on Hamngatan, and walk to the park. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the blossom tunnel and tilt the phone upward. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the canopy and the path in one frame. A 2x telephoto setting suits a tighter shot of the blossom against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Kungsträdgården (blossom avenue inside the park, shooting up into the canopy). A pink cherry-blossom canopy over the park's paths, best framed by looking upward toward the blossoms against the sky. The middle of the park lies to the south. From here you look up through the tunnel of pink blossom over the paths, with the sky showing between the branches.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone close to your chest and point it up so the branches arch over the top of the frame. Turn on gridlines to keep the avenue symmetrical. For a different composition, try the oversized chess pieces in the foreground with blossom above, or the swans on the water with the city buildings behind. Both are in other parts of the park.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the blossom to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out the pink. Live Photos can catch petals moving in the breeze.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late April, when the blossom is usually out. Go early in the morning to beat the crowds. Outside spring, the fountains, trees and winter ice rink are the main subjects.

text.access_note: Kungsträdgården is an open public park, but events can change what is on show, so check the official site before you go.

name: Monteliusvägen viewpoint
label: Monteliusvägen
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mariaberget' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Mariaberget' (way/24606774): middle (383 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/144024295: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description:
Monteliusvägen is a cobbled path with a view across the water to Stockholm's City Hall. From the lookout at Mariaberget you see the City Hall across the water. From along the Monteliusvägen path, Gamla Stan's rooftops and spires and Riddarholmen come into view, with the City Hall tower off to one side. The cobbled lane and the houses along it make a good foreground, so the picture feels like a street scene as well as a view.

One photo guide says the lookout at Mariaberget is the main spot, but suggests walking on to the far side of the path. From there you can include the cobbles and the houses, which makes a more interesting composition. The best spot along the path is a matter of taste, so take a few steps between shots and compare. If you want wider, more open views over the water and the skyline from a different angle, Skinnarviksberget is another viewpoint nearby. It is informal rock with no railing, so take care there.

The path is not salted in winter, and the boardwalk sections can be slippery, so wear shoes with grip in cold weather. Stay behind the edge while you take photos, and keep the phone strap or wrist loop on if you have one.
text.geographic_location: Along a path that looks across the water to the City Hall and Gamla Stan.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot. Guides give different approach routes (some mention Bastugatan steps, others Klevgränd or Mariatorget), so check the map before you set out. Check the name Mariaberget on the map too. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the City Hall across the water. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) when you walk to the far side of the path and want the cobbled lane, the houses and the view in one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the City Hall tower or Gamla Stan's spires.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Mariaberget (the observation area at the main lookout on the path, then continuing on to the far side of the path). The City Hall across the water, with the cobblestone path and the houses lining it in the foreground. After your first photos, walk on to the far side of the path to include the cobbled lane and the houses lining it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the cobbled path or the row of houses along the lower third, with the City Hall across the water in the upper part. Keep the horizon level, because the water makes any tilt obvious. For a second picture, from along the Monteliusvägen path, take in Gamla Stan and Riddarholmen and let the City Hall tower sit to one side. Skinnarviksberget is an alternative if you want a wider skyline view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the City Hall or the sky to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky looks washed out. Use the ultra-wide lens only when the lane really helps the picture, because it can make distant landmarks look small. In low light, night mode helps, but rest your elbows on something steady and wait for it to finish.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: There is no set best time. In winter, avoid icy mornings, because the path is not salted and the boardwalk sections can be slippery.

text.access_note: Open public walking path with no entry charge; take care on the boardwalk sections, which can be slippery in winter.

name: Slussen and the view over Gamla Stan
label: Slussen
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q97578035: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description: Slussen is the busy meeting point at the northern edge of Södermalm, right beside Gamla Stan. It has been a crossing place between the southern roads and the waterways linking Lake Mälaren with the Baltic Sea for centuries, and the first lock here dates from 1642. The area is in the middle of a big rebuild. Work began in 2016 and completion is scheduled for 2027, so you may see cranes, hoardings or temporary walkways in your photos. The newer features give you good things to frame. The Golden Bridge (Guldbron), officially Slussbron, joins Södermalm to Gamla Stan for traffic, pedestrians and cyclists, and it opened on 26 October 2020. The new water channels and low bridges of Vattentorget, opened in phases in 2022 and 2024, add water and lines to the scene. The 1935 lock was the last major one before the current rebuild. The idea is a wide, open view with water, bridges and the old town beyond. Keep the horizon level, include some foreground such as railings or paving to give depth, and wait a moment for people or vehicles to clear if you want a calmer frame. Expect the layout to keep changing while the works continue.
text.geographic_location: Slussen is at the northern edge of Södermalm, next to Gamla Stan, where the locks link Lake Mälaren and the Baltic Sea.
text.directions_text: Head for Slussen, at the northern edge of Södermalm next to Gamla Stan. Because of the building works, follow any signs and temporary walkways rather than the exact line on the map. The phone icon on the map is about 60 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole scene. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the bridge and sky, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out rooftops and details across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 60 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. Face east, with the subject straight ahead of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower line. Use railings, paving or the water's edge as a foreground. With the default lens (1x), keep the straight edges of bridges and buildings parallel to the grid so they don't lean. Take one wide shot, then zoom in for a tighter shot of Gamla Stan's rooftops.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the buildings to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps some colour. If the light is low, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body or a railing to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or around sunset usually gives softer light, and after dark the lit-up bridges and water can look good in night mode.

text.access_note: Slussen is an open public area, but the redevelopment may close or change some routes, so check the official site before you go.

name: Nordic Museum
label: Nordic Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Djurgårdsbron' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Djurgårdsbron' (way/421206372): middle (67 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/348345482: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Nordic Museum' (169 m across).

text.description:
The Nordic Museum (Nordiska museet) is a large, castle-like building on Djurgården, the island in central Stockholm. It tells the everyday cultural history of Sweden from 1520 to the present day. Artur Hazelius, who also founded the open-air museum Skansen, started the collection in the 1870s. The building we see now was designed by Isak Gustaf Clason and finished in 1907, after a construction period of 19 years. It was meant to be even bigger, about three times the size that was actually built. Its look comes from Dutch-influenced Danish Renaissance buildings such as Frederiksborg Palace, and brick and granite give the walls a warm, solid texture. Inside, a huge main hall 126 metres long runs up to the roof. It is dominated by a giant sculpture of King Gustav Vasa.

It photographs well from across the water. From the Strandvägen end of Djurgårdsbron you can fit the palace-style facade into one frame with the water in front of it, which gives a calm, uncluttered foreground. Stand at the bridge abutment, keep your phone level and let the building fill the middle of the picture. If you have time, Skeppsholmsbron shows the museum with Djurgården's trees and the harbour around it. Galärparken gives a waterfront view across Djurgården toward Strandvägen and Skeppsholmen, with the museum nearby.
text.geographic_location: On Djurgården, the island in central Stockholm, just across the water from the Strandvägen waterfront. The best view of it is from Djurgårdsbron, the bridge that leads onto the island.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are listed for this spot, so head for Strandvägen in central Stockholm and then go by taxi or hired scooter to the Strandvägen end of Djurgårdsbron. From there the museum is about 4 minutes on foot to the south, across the bridge and onto Djurgården. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole facade across the water. Switch to telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) for the towers and roofline, and keep the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the alternative viewpoints, where you may be closer and want more sky and water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Djurgårdsbron (Strandvägen end, from the bridge abutment). The museum's palace-style facade seen across the water from the Strandvägen side of the bridge. From here you look south across the water to the museum's palace-style facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the building up so its vertical edges run parallel to the grid lines. Put the facade in the middle of the frame, with a band of water along the bottom. If you want a different view, try Skeppsholmsbron or Galärparken.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus and exposure. Because you are looking south, the sky behind the building can be bright, so drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is washing out, but check that the facade does not become too dark. Take a few frames in case a passer-by or vehicle crosses the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Looking south, the midday sun is ahead of you, so around late morning to early afternoon expect backlight on the facade. An overcast day gives softer, more even light, and on a sunny day a small exposure adjustment helps. A clear, calm day gives the best reflections in the water.

text.access_note: The bridge viewpoint is a public place, but check the official site before you go if you also want to go inside the museum.

name: Riddarholmen Church
label: Riddarholmen Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Evert Taubes terrass' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Evert Taubes Terrass' (way/26224594): middle (190 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/23841420: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Riddarholm Church' (74 m across).

text.description:
Riddarholmen Church is one of the oldest buildings in Stockholm, with parts dating back to the late 13th century, when it was built as a Franciscan friary. After the Reformation it became a Lutheran church. The congregation was dissolved in 1807, and today the church is used only for burials and commemorations. Most Swedish monarchs are laid to rest here. The church mixes Gothic and baroque styles. The slim cast-iron spire is the part you will spot from far away. It replaced an earlier spire that was destroyed by lightning in 1835.

The church photographs best as part of a wider scene. From Evert Taube's Terrace on the west side of the island, you look over Riddarfjärden bay to Stockholm City Hall and the Söder heights, with the spire rising on the island. Guides name this as the island's finest open view and the spot most often chosen for sunset pictures. For a close portrait of the building, two other places work well. Birger Jarls torg shows the whole church front and spire, and from the northern part of the island you can also fit in the pink Stenbock palaces. Schering Rosenhanes gränd shows the church up a cobbled lane, with the winding path leading the eye towards it.

The church interior is closed in the cooler months, so plan for outside shots and check the official site before you go if you hope to go in.
text.geographic_location: On the island of Riddarholmen in central Stockholm, close to the Royal Palace. The terrace sits on the island's west shore, facing Riddarfjärden bay.
text.directions_text: No station is listed for this spot, so start from the Royal Palace and head for the island of Riddarholmen next door. From there the church is a short stroll to the east, about 3 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the bay, City Hall and the sky together. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the spire or City Hall on its own.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Evert Taubes terrass (west side of Riddarholmen island). Riddarfjärden bay in front, with Stockholm City Hall and Söder heights across the water and the church spire rising on the island. From here your photo takes in Riddarfjärden bay in front of you, with Stockholm City Hall and the Söder heights across the water and the church spire rising on the island.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the water along the lower third, so the skyline and spire sit above it. For a close-up of the church itself, walk to Birger Jarls torg for the whole front and spire. Schering Rosenhanes gränd gives a more intimate shot of the church framed by cobblestones.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the far shore to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sunset colours don't wash out. If the light fades, try night mode and rest your phone on the terrace railing or a wall to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, per guides, when the view across the bay is at its best.

text.access_note: The island and its outdoor viewpoints are open public space, but the church itself is a royal burial church that is closed in the cooler months, so check the official site before you go.

name: Nationalmuseum
label: Nationalmuseum
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/24968329: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'National Museum of Fine Arts' (127 m across).

text.description:
Nationalmuseum is Sweden's national gallery of fine arts, standing on the Blasieholmen peninsula in central Stockholm. The building was designed by the German architect Friedrich August Stüler, who also designed the Neues Museum in Berlin. It took from 1844 to 1866 to build and draws on northern Italian Renaissance architecture. The outside is clad in Swedish limestone and looks fairly closed and calm, which makes it an easy, tidy subject for a phone: long, even lines, and a pale surface that picks up the colour of the sky.

The museum was founded in 1792 as the Royal Museum, and the present building opened in 1866. After a renovation it reopened on 13 October 2018, and the restored windows and ceiling lanterns brought daylight back into the galleries. The outline of the building is about 127 m across, so it is a wide subject.

Take one wide shot of the whole building first, then move closer for details such as the windows and the stonework. Keep the phone level so the walls don't lean. If you want to photograph the inside, check the official site before you go, as access and photo rules there may differ from the outside.
text.geographic_location: Nationalmuseum is on the Blasieholmen peninsula in central Stockholm.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Blasieholmen in central Stockholm. From there the museum is about 103 m to the south-east, about 2 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 60 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole building. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if passers-by or a lack of space stop you stepping back, and use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details of the façade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 60 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. From here the long front fits in the frame without a steep upward tilt.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line them up with the edges of the building so the walls stay upright. Leave a little sky above the roofline, and include some foreground to give a sense of scale. For a second shot, zoom in on a row of windows or a corner of the limestone.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the pale limestone keeps its detail rather than turning white. Take a few shots with slightly different exposure.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft light earlier or later in the day is usually kinder to pale stone than harsh midday sun. Check the weather on the day, because an overcast sky gives an even, but flatter, result.

text.access_note: The stand-here point is outside the museum; check local signs for any restrictions. Entry to the museum and any photo rules inside are not covered here, so check the official site before you go.

name: Mårten Trotzigs gränd
label: Mårten Trotzigs gränd
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mårten Trotzigs gränd' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/27347607: the middle of the OpenStreetMap line 'Mårten Trotzigs Gränd' (19 m long).

text.description: Mårten Trotzigs gränd is a short stepped lane in Gamla stan, the old town, and it has a good claim to being the narrowest street in Stockholm. It climbs from Västerlånggatan and Järntorget up to Prästgatan and Tyska Stallplan. Its 37 steps tighten from a comfortable width to just 90 centimetres at the narrowest point, so the tall old walls seem to close in as you look up. That squeezed, rising shape is what makes it such a good phone photo: the steps lead the eye straight up the frame and the walls give it depth. The lane is named after Mårten Trotzig, a merchant born in Wittenberg who came to Stockholm in 1581 and bought property here in 1597 and 1599. Older names for it include "Narrow Stairs Alley", recorded in 1544. It was closed off in the mid-19th century and not reopened until 1945, and the present name was confirmed by the city in 1949. For the best picture, stand at the foot of the steps at the Västerlånggatan end and shoot upwards. The view from the top looks flatter than the lane really is, so it is not worth photographing from there. The lane is so narrow that two people can barely pass, so be ready to wait a moment for others to clear the frame. Early morning is the quietest time.
text.geographic_location: In Gamla stan, the old town of Stockholm, running up from Västerlånggatan and Järntorget to Prästgatan and Tyska Stallplan.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the square Järntorget in Gamla stan and look for the lane leading up from Västerlånggatan near Järntorget. If you are coming from elsewhere in Stockholm, go to Gamla stan by taxi and walk in from Järntorget. Take the lane's lower end, at Västerlånggatan, as your starting point. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which shows the steps and both walls in one frame. Try the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the height, but stay close to the centre of the lane so the walls do not lean in too much. Avoid zooming in, as it flattens the sense of narrowness.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From the foot of the steps, the lane rises directly away from you, with the tall old walls closing in on both sides and the narrowest section receding toward the top.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the centre of the steps on the middle line so the walls look balanced on either side. Hold the phone at chest height and keep it level so the walls stay straight. Wait for a gap in passers-by, or include one person on the steps to give a sense of scale. Only this low viewpoint is recommended; the view from the top end is flatter.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the steps partway up to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the bright sky at the top does not wash out. Take a few shots in a row, as people will move through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before Västerlånggatan fills with visitors.

text.access_note: The lane is an open public passage, but building work can close it for short periods, so check on arrival; the steps are narrow and not suitable for wheelchairs or pushchairs.

name: Skeppsholmen Bridge and its crowns
label: Skeppsholmsbron
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/660513753: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Skeppsholmsbron' (183 m across).

text.description: Skeppsholmen Bridge links the Blasieholmen peninsula with the island of Skeppsholmen in central Stockholm. It has five arches, is 165 metres long and carries a roadway with a narrow pathway on each side. The present bridge opened in 1861 and was the first forged iron bridge built in Sweden, made by Motala Verkstad. At the midpoint sit the two Gilded Crowns, a symbol of Sweden and its Royal Family. They give the bridge a clear focal point, and the arches and railings give you lines to build a picture around. There has been a crossing here since the 1630s, when a wooden bridge was built for the navy's move to the island. The current bridge was listed as a historical landmark in 1935. For a phone photo, treat it as two pictures. First, take the whole bridge, with the arches and the water, so the structure and its length show. Second, take a close shot of one of the crowns against the sky or the water behind. Keep the horizon level with the gridlines on, as the bridge's long edges look odd when tilted. Wait a moment for people to pass if you want a clear railing, or leave them in to show scale. Take a few frames, because the pathways are narrow and people keep moving.
text.geographic_location: In central Stockholm, on the bridge that connects Blasieholmen with the island of Skeppsholmen. The Gilded Crowns are at the middle of the bridge.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop right at this spot, so start from Blasieholmen in central Stockholm and walk onto the bridge towards Skeppsholmen. If you are coming from elsewhere in the city, head to Blasieholmen and finish on foot. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the bridge and its surroundings. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the full run of arches in one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a close shot of a crown.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stay on the pathway and out of the roadway.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: For a wide shot, use the gridlines to keep the railing and the water edge level, and let the arches lead the eye along the bridge. For a detail shot, zoom in on one crown and keep the sky or water behind it plain so it stands out. Take a few frames so you have one with few people in it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the crown to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the gilding is not washed out against a bright sky. Turn on the gridlines to keep the bridge straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early or late in the day usually gives softer light on the gilding and fewer people on the pathways, but any clear time works for the arches.

text.access_note: The bridge carries a roadway and pathways, so you can walk across it, but check the official site before you go in case of works or closures.

name: Stockholm Cathedral (Storkyrkan)
label: Storkyrkan
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/8049504: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Great Church' (93 m across).

text.description: Storkyrkan, also called Stockholm Cathedral, is the oldest church in Stockholm. It sits at the highest point of Gamla stan, wedged between Stockholm Palace and the old square of Stortorget. It was dedicated in 1306, though building probably began in the 13th century. Inside, it keeps much of its late medieval character. Outside, it looks uniformly Baroque, the result of big changes made in the 18th century. That mix of old history and tidy Baroque walls is what makes it satisfying to photograph: the façade is calm and solid, and it sits among other grand buildings of the same period. The church has long royal links. It was used for coronations for centuries, and Crown Princess Victoria married there in 2010. Beside the east wall, facing Slottsbacken, stands a statue of the reformer Olaus Petri, unveiled in 1898. It makes a good foreground detail. In the pavement there, lines mark where an older church choir once stood. A small courtyard lies just south of the church, with wrought iron gates and statues on the west gate posts dating from 1675. The church is surrounded on three sides by streets, with the courtyard to the south. Plan on tall, angled shots and on detail pictures rather than one wide view. Check the official site before you go if you want to photograph inside.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Gamla stan, the old town of Stockholm, between Stockholm Palace and Stortorget, next to the Stock Exchange Building.
text.directions_text: Make your way to Gamla stan and aim for Stockholm Palace or the square of Stortorget; the church lies between the two. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x), because you are close to a large building. Switch to the default lens (1x) for calmer, more natural-looking shots. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the Olaus Petri statue, the gates and the roofline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line them up with the walls and corners so the building does not lean. Hold the phone level and step back as far as the street allows before tilting up. If you want a people-free foreground, try a low angle with the statue or the pavement lines near the east side.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the church wall to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the façade keeps its colour and detail. Take a couple of frames in case a passer-by walks into the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or later in the afternoon usually gives softer light and quieter streets, but check how the light falls on the day.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the surrounding streets, but this is a working church, so check the official site before you go for visiting times, any entry rules and whether photography inside is allowed.

name: German Church
label: German Church
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/8049509: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'German Church' (56 m across).

text.description:
The German Church (Tyska kyrkan) stands in the middle of Gamla stan, packed in among narrow streets, and its tall brick tower is the part you will notice first. The tower and copper-covered spire together reach 96 metres and were finished in 1878, after a fire destroyed the earlier tower. The church grew out of a medieval guild building belonging to German merchants, which is why the church is known as the German Church. It was enlarged to its present two-nave form in 1638-1642.

It photographs well because of the setting. The streets around it are tight, so you rarely get a clean view of the whole building, but that works in your favour: the spire rises above the old rooftops and makes a strong vertical shot. Look closely at the details too. Over the northern gate facing Tyska Brinken there is a gilded image of the patron saint, St Gertrude, and the tower carries Neogothic gargoyles shaped like grotesque animals.

For your phone, expect to tilt the camera upwards, which can make the tower lean inwards. Keep the phone upright and use the gridlines to line up the walls. If you want the whole spire, step back along the lane and use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) carefully. For the carved details, use the telephoto lens instead. Because the lanes are narrow, shots are often best taken early in the day, when there are fewer people in the frame.
text.geographic_location: In Gamla stan, the old town in central Stockholm, closely surrounded by Tyska Brinken, Kindstugatan, Svartmangatan and Prästgatan.
text.directions_text: No nearby station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from Gamla stan, the old town, and walk into the lanes around Tyska Brinken. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the church in its street setting. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you want the tower and the narrow lane together, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the gargoyles, the gilded saint and the portal.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Because you are so close, you will mostly capture the lower walls, doorways and details here, and the tower will need a tilt upwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the phone as upright as you can, so the walls do not lean in. Use the tower as a vertical line against the sky, with the lane or old rooftops at the edge. For a full view of the spire, walk a little way back along one of the lanes and use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x), keeping the tower away from the very edge of the frame where it stretches.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brickwork to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not turn white. In narrow lanes, the shaded walls and bright sky can be very different, so check the screen before you shoot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning usually means fewer people in the lanes. A clear day gives a clean sky behind the spire. Dusk can be good for the tower against a darker sky, and night mode can help if the lane is dim.

text.access_note: The church is in the middle of the old town and the lanes around it are open public space, but visiting inside depends on the season and services, so check the official site before you go.
